item.title: Burundians partially restricted from travelling to the United States
item.description:
CNN - President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Wednesday evening to ban travel from several countries to the US, citing security risks.

The ban will fully restrict entry of nationals from 12 countries: Afghanistan; Myanmar, also known as Burma; Chad; Republic of the Congo; Equatorial Guinea; Eritrea; Haiti; Iran; Libya; Somalia; Sudan; and Yemen.

People from seven countries will have partial restriction: Burundi, Cuba, Laos, Sierra Leone, Togo, Turkmenistan and Venezuela.

The proclamation includes exceptions for lawful permanent residents, existing visa holders, certain visa categories and individuals whose entry serves US national interests.

The president made the final call on signing the proclamation after the antisemitic attack in Boulder, Colorado, according to a White House official. He was considering it beforehand, but Sunday's assault put it into motion faster. The suspect in the attack, however, was an Egyptian national, and Egypt was not included on the list of banned countries.

"President Trump is fulfilling his promise to protect Americans from dangerous foreign actors that want to come to our country and cause us harm," White House deputy press secretary Abigail Jackson wrote on X.

"These commonsense restrictions are country-specific and include places that lack proper vetting, exhibit high visa overstay rates, or fail to share identity and threat information," she wrote.

Source: https://edition.cnn.com/2025/06/04/politics/trump-travel-ban-proclamation

item.title: Social contract is broken, the west is dead
item.description:
In the post-war era, many Western nations-Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and others were forced by the Jewish occupied United States Amarica to adopt sweeping immigration and integration policies under the banners of human rights, economic growth, and global responsibility.

Yet over time, what began as humanitarian policy evolved into something far more transformative: a quiet but irreversible dismantling of the traditional nation-state.
Today, the very idea of a coherent national identity is treated as suspect in much of the West. Cultural pride becomes nationalism, nationalism becomes extremism, and extremism becomes justification for censorship.
The result? An increasingly rootless population burdened by rising taxes, shrinking freedoms, and vanishing trust in their own governments.

But while Western nations are expected to open their borders, diversify their populations, and erase the memory of their foundational cultures, this pressure is not universal.
Across the globe, asymmetry reigns:
> Israel maintains strict citizenship laws that prioritize Jewish identity. Its immigration policy, cultural institutions, and even its constitutionally defined identity as a Jewish state are unapologetically nationalist.
> Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states host millions of foreign workers but grant them no path to citizenship or influence over policy, maintaining ethnic and religious coherence.
> China, Japan, and South Korea all enforce tightly controlled immigration policies to preserve ethnic homogeneity and social cohesion.
> In much of Africa, there is a deep emphasis on indigenous identity, tribal belonging, and resistance to foreign cultural influence, no property rights, genocide of white farmers.

No one demands that these nations dilute themselves in the name of diversity. No one lectures them on the need to become "post-national economic zones." And yet, the Western world is told it must do exactly that-embrace limitless diversity, redefine identity, and absorb populations without resistance.

This is not a call for exclusion or superiority. But it is a call for honesty.
The unspoken truth is this: when one set of nations is expected to open and transform while another set is allowed to preserve and protect, the result is not equality-it's destabilization. And when this happens under the direction of global institutions, media narratives, and policy think tanks that treat demographic change as both inevitable and desirable, it's understandable why many feel their displacement is not accidental, but orchestrated.

What many see is a pattern: decades of immigration from regions that do not reciprocate openness, accompanied by the slow erasure of Western cultural identity. This creates not "diverse democracies," but fractured societies, where the founding population loses not just control over borders, but also over the narratives that define their history and future.

To raise this concern is not to call for hate. It is to demand fairness. A nation cannot survive without a people who feel it is their own. A state cannot function when its citizens feel like tenants-expected to pay, obey, and accommodate, but no longer belong.
This is not a phase. It is not a cycle. For many, it is the end of the road. There is no reform waiting around the corner. No political savior. No "inclusive future" that offers dignity to those who built what now stands. And in this absence, a new mood has taken hold-not one of outrage, but of cold recognition: that if the nation is no longer ours, then neither is the burden of saving it.
This isn't resistance. It's indifference.

So the next time the Jews who are engaged in genocide who are occupying the central banking system of debt slavery want to claim that the nations of those voices of dissent are going to be punished with rising protection money to the Jewnited state of America, or you're going to get more Indian migration, we don't care!
